You want the `check: true` kwarg to run_command, because recent versions of Meson emit a deprecation warning if you don't specify some value of `check`.

It's best to use "true", because that would ideally have been the default all along -- if those commands error out for some crazy reason Meson can error out if the information is required.

If you're going to use Meson's documented support for f-strings, which was added in Meson 0.58, you might want to set that in the `project()` function as `meson_version: '>=0.58.0'` so that Meson can error out on older versions and tell the user to "upgrade Meson".

It's a pretty recent version and e.g. not available in Debian stable's official repositories. It's of course trivial to upgrade it with `pip install`, but it's quite easy to imagine people trying the version from the Debian repositories first, then having it fail, so letting them know the reason is because they have an old version of Meson is useful information.

I'll try to explain my changes and how I think they relate to the formula above. But all my changes revolve around : add a scaling factor where needed in already existing code / computation formulas.

The original code is (if the window is X11) :

```
local = g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() - m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_vRealPosition.goalv();
```

I understand `g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal()` as `coords`.
I understand `m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_vRealPosition.goalv()` as `windowpos`.

I scaled this whole expression by `m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_fX11SurfaceScaledBy` which I understand as `scale`.

The result is : 

```
local = (g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() - m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_vRealPosition.goalv()) * m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_fX11SurfaceScaledBy;
```

Which corresponds to `(coords - windowpos) * scale` in my understanding. After several tests it works for the initial touch down, which is what this function is all about. 

However this function also prepares another, for touch moves, and stores a `touchSurfaceOrigin`. 

The original code uses two distincts paths if the window is X11 or not to compute the `local` variable. In the X11 case this variable units are X11 scaled units, in the other case the units are global screen scale units. What is important is that they differ.

The original code modifies this variable this way : 

```
m_sTouchData.touchSurfaceOrigin = g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() - local;
```

As `getMouseCoordsInternal()` is in global screen scale units and local may be in one or the other unit, I was forced to compute `touchSurfaceOrigin` differently in the two cases.

The modified code in the case if an X11 window becomes : 

```
m_sTouchData.touchSurfaceOrigin = (g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() * m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_fX11SurfaceScaledBy) - local;
```

`local` is already in X11 units, I have to change the coords again accordingly. (or use a variable and scale it once and for all, but I chose to modify the original code as few as possible). 

All this code prepares what will happen next in `onTouchMove()` that I describe in the other conversation.

The original code is : 

```
const auto local = g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() - m_sTouchData.touchSurfaceOrigin;
```

I changed it to take into account the case where the window is X11 : 

```
 auto local = g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() - m_sTouchData.touchSurfaceOrigin;
 if (m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_bIsX11) {
      local = (g_pInputManager->getMouseCoordsInternal() * m_sTouchData.touchFocusWindow->m_fX11SurfaceScaledBy) - m_sTouchData.touchSurfaceOrigin;
}
```

All I do is to scale anew `getMouseCoordsInternal()` to X11 units. The origin has already been scaled to these units in `onTouchDown`. This could be refactored to avoid computing `local` twice, but once again I wanted to introduce as few changes as possible.

The formula would therefore pass from `coords - origin` to `coords * scale - origin`.

I tested this also and it works as expected, correcting the bug.

Should I introduce the `- windowpos` to have the formula `(coords - windowpos) * scale - origin` ? The original code does not do it, so I'm unsure, but I do not think so. This is already "included" in the `origin` calculation, and indeed not done in the original code. 

Furthermore, when introducing it, the tests fail as soon as the X11 window is not in the top left corner of the screen. My tests are done using Krita and zooming/moving the drawing with touch, and also by running `xev` that reports X events and coordinates. 

I have been running these tests on a debug build running inside another instance if Hyprland and also in release mode. I have been running it with these corrections for three days now and have encountered no problems with X11 apps.

In my case, I'm developing a plugin for Hyprland that acts as a proxy for events. This plugin allows you to run scripts in Bash, Python, etc., when event hooks are called. in hyprutils, .expired and operator bool are two different checks, but here will behave the same. That's why the shorter version is better.

`.expired()` checks if it's not possible to make a `SP` anymore.
`operator bool` checks if the pointer is still reference-able.

Difference is in the ~dtor of an object that is owned by a SP. You can't make SPs anymore (because that would resurrect the container) but you can still reference the pointer via `->` because the actual object is not deleted yet.

>no we want it here, otherwise sync releaser wont be reset until the new buffer arrives which causes it to become a bit delayish.

<details>
<summary>The buffer release is supposed to be delayed so that there is always a valid buffer during scanout</summary>
Basically, once a buffer is committed to KMS (using `output->commit();`), it is locked until the next frame.
Then in the new frame's attemptDirectScanout, if we have a new buffer to commit, we will commit it to KMS and then the AQ backend will unlock the original buffer once the new one is being scanned out
</details>

Also `current.buffer->buffer->lockedByBackend` will never be set here because it is only set after a KMS `output->commit()` of the surface buffer, which only happens in attemptDirectScanout in the _next_ onMonitorFrame after a surface commit provides a new/different buffer

PR desc:

> To ensure that we can't get into a situation, where neither locked or finished is sent, I added an event loop timer of 5 seconds that sends finished in case the client wasn't able to create and commit lock surfaces within that time.

See also the comment I added. The timer has two purposes:
It is there so that a client can't just create a new lock and then do nothing (thus essentially inhibiting a new session-lock). And with this PR, in addition, the rendering for lockscreen and workspaces is tied to `locked` and `finished`. Thus it also serves as a fallback if for example the session-lock client fails to create a surface for one of the outputs.

This is the relevant protocol section:
> The compositor may wait for the client to create and render session lock surfaces before sending the locked event to avoid displaying intermediate blank frames. However, it must impose a reasonable time limit if waiting and send the locked event as soon as the hard requirements described above can be met if the time limit expires. Clients should immediately create lock surfaces for all outputs on creation of this object to make this possible.

Regarding the validity check, I'd like to share my reasoning for adding it, but I'm happy to remove it if you still feel it's unnecessary.

My main concern is making the code robust through defensive programming. While `main.cpp` currently ensures `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is set, that dependency is external to this class. If the startup logic in `main.cpp` ever changes, or if this class is used in a different context in the future, this check prevents a potential null pointer bug from surfacing here. It makes the class more self-contained and reliable. I find it's a small price to pay for future stability.

If you agree to keep the check, let's decide on the style. I think you suggested `!XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR[0]`. This would actually cause a crash if the variable is null due to the `&&`. Perhaps you meant `if (!XDG_RUNTIME_DIR || !XDG_RUNTIME_DIR[0])`?
